warmup.q: fun total(amounts: MutableList<Number>): Double only reads the list. You call it with cents: MutableList<Int>. What happens?
options: It compiles: an Int is a Number, so a list of ints is a list of numbers
It doesn't compile, and the only fix is to copy cents into a new MutableList<Number>
It doesn't compile, but MutableList<out Number> in the signature fixes it
It compiles, and fails at run time when total reads the first element
warmup.why: MutableList is invariant, because it both reads and writes E, so a MutableList<Int> is not a MutableList<Number>. But total only reads, so it can ask for an out-projection: MutableList<out Number> accepts a list of any subtype of Number. Copying works too, but you don't need it. Option one is the intuition that lesson 3 of this track disproved.

sections.h: MutableList and Array can't pick a side, so you project them
sections.html:
Lessons 4 and 5 of this track put the variance on the class: Feed<out T> only hands values out, Sink<in T> only takes them in. Many types can't do that. MutableList<E> has get(): E and add(element: E). Array<T> has get and set. T sits in both positions, so the class must stay invariant, and lesson 3 showed what goes wrong when Java arrays pretend otherwise.

The trouble is that one function rarely uses both sides. Here is the copy example from the Kotlin docs, first without any variance:

fun copyRow(from: Array<Any>, to: Array<Any>) { for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i] }

copyRow(amounts, row)     // amounts is an Array<Int>
Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Array<Int>', but 'Array<Any>' was expected.

Kotlin refuses for a good reason. If copyRow could see an Array<Int> as an Array<Any>, it could write a String into it. But copyRow never writes to from. It only reads. So you tell the compiler that, right where the type is used:

Java
// Java arrays are covariant, so Object[] already accepts an Integer[]
static void copyRow(Object[] from, Object[] to) {
    for (int i = 0; i < from.length; i++) to[i] = from[i];   // the JVM checks each store
}

copyRow(amounts, row);              // fine
copyRow(amounts, new String[3]);    // compiles, then throws ArrayStoreException
Kotlin
fun copyRow(from: Array<out Any>, to: Array<Any>) {
    for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i]   // get() on Array<out Any> returns Any
}

copyRow(amounts, row)                       // fine: Array<Int> fits Array<out Any>
copyRow(amounts, arrayOfNulls<String>(3))   // compile error: Array<String?> is not an Array<Any>

Array<out Any> is a type projection. You haven't changed Array. You've asked for a narrower view of it, for one parameter: an array of some subtype of Any that this function will only read. Through that view get returns Any, and set is gone:

from[0] = "EUR"
Receiver type 'Array<out Any>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun set(index: Int, value: T): Unit'.

Writing the variance where a type is used is called use-site variance. Java's wildcards are the same idea, and they are the only kind of variance Java has. Arrays are the odd case on the Java side: there are no wildcards for arrays, because every Java array has been covariant since Java 1.0 and the JVM checks each store at run time instead. Kotlin's Array<out Any> compiles to a plain Object[].

The figure shows the three ways to look at one invariant type.

sections.h: An out-projection is a read view, and Java spells it ? extends
sections.html:
The projection you'll write most often is on MutableList. Here is a function that totals any mutable list of numbers:

Java
static double total(List<? extends Number> amounts) {
    double sum = 0;
    for (Number a : amounts) sum += a.doubleValue();   // reads come out as Number
    return sum;
}

total(cents);    // a List<Integer>
total(rates);    // a List<Double>
Kotlin
fun total(amounts: MutableList<out Number>): Double {
    var sum = 0.0
    for (a in amounts) sum += a.toDouble()      // reads come out as Number
    return sum
}

total(cents)     // a MutableList<Int>
total(rates)     // a MutableList<Double>

Read MutableList<out Number> as "a mutable list of some subtype of Number, and I don't know which". That unknown is why writing is forbidden. The list might be cents, a MutableList<Int>. Adding 2.5 would put a Double into a list of ints. So both compilers refuse every call that takes the element type:

amounts.add(0)
Kotlin: Receiver type 'MutableList<out Number>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'.
Java:   incompatible types: int cannot be converted to CAP#1

Even add(0) fails, though 0 is a fine Int. The compiler doesn't know the list holds ints. CAP#1 is javac's name for that unknown: a captured type, a placeholder for "the one real element type of this particular list". Kotlin prints it as CapturedType(out Number), for example when you try val x: Int = amounts[0]. Nothing you can write is known to be a subtype of the placeholder, so nothing goes in.

Members that don't take an E still work. size, isEmpty(), removeAt(0) and clear() all compile through the view, as lesson 4 showed. A projection limits which types flow in. It does not stop the list from changing.

You need this only for invariant types. Kotlin's read-only List is already declared List<out E>, so a plain List<Number> parameter accepts a List<Int>. Write List<out Number> and the compiler warns that the projection is redundant. You'll see that warning in this lesson's lab.

It only reads, so it asks for an out-projection. */ fun total(amounts: MutableList<out Number>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (a in amounts) sum += a.toDouble() // reads come out as Number // amounts.add(0) // wrong move 1: no add() through an out-projection return sum } fun main() { val cents: MutableList<Int> = mutableListOf(1_200, 350, 99) val rates: MutableList<Double> = mutableListOf(0.5, 1.25) println("cents: ${total(cents)}, rates: ${total(rates)}") val view: MutableList<out Number> = cents // the same projection on a variable view.removeAt(0) // still allowed: removeAt takes an Int, not a T println("after removeAt through the view: $cents") // Wrong move 2: no projection, so a MutableList<Int> is not a MutableList<Number>. // val strict: MutableList<Number> = cents }

(Java: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to CAP#1), and the strict assignment with expected 'MutableList<Number>', actual 'MutableList<Int>' (Java: List<Integer> cannot be converted to List<Number>). List<Number> compiles with no projection; List<out Number> compiles with the warning Projection is redundant: the corresponding type parameter of 'List<out Number>' has the same variance.

sections.h: An in-projection is a write view, and Java spells it ? super
sections.html:
Now flip the direction. This helper appends zero-amount placeholder lines. It only ever writes Ints:

Java
static void padWithZeros(List<? super Integer> target, int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(0);
}

padWithZeros(ints, 1);       // List<Integer>
padWithZeros(numbers, 2);    // List<Number>
padWithZeros(anything, 2);   // List<Object>
Kotlin
fun padWithZeros(target: MutableList<in Int>, count: Int) {
    repeat(count) { target.add(0) }
}

padWithZeros(ints, 1)        // MutableList<Int>
padWithZeros(numbers, 2)     // MutableList<Number>
padWithZeros(anything, 2)    // MutableList<Any>

MutableList<in Int> means "a mutable list of Int or of some supertype of Int". Every such list accepts an Int, so add(0) is safe. Reading is the side that gets weaker. An element might be the 2.5 or the "EUR" that was already in the list, so the only thing the compiler can promise is Any? (Java: Object):

val firstInt: Int = target[0]
Kotlin: Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Int', actual 'CapturedType(in Int)'.
Java:   incompatible types: CAP#1 cannot be converted to Integer

A MutableList<Double> is rejected at the call, because it can't take an Int: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<Double>', but 'MutableList<in Int>' was expected.

The JDK's utility methods are written this way, and calling them from Kotlin is a good way to learn the mapping. Two of them from java.util.Collections, and the same contracts in Kotlin:

Java
public static <T> void fill(List<? super T> list, T obj) { /* ... */ }
public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) { /* ... */ }
Kotlin
fun <T> fill(list: MutableList<in T>, obj: T) { /* ... */ }
fun <T> copy(dest: MutableList<in T>, src: List<T>) { /* ... */ }

Pass the wrong thing to the real Collections.copy from Kotlin, and the error shows how Kotlin reads Java's wildcards:

java.util.Collections.copy(ints, listOf("a"))
Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'List<String>', but '(Mutable)List<out Int!>!' was expected.

Java's ? extends became out. The rule in the Kotlin docs is that Foo<? extends Bar> becomes Foo<out Bar!>! and Foo<? super Bar> becomes Foo<in Bar!>!. The ! marks a platform type (Kotlin can't tell whether Java allows null), and (Mutable)List means Kotlin can't tell whether Java will modify the list. It works the other way too: a Kotlin parameter MutableList<in T> compiles to Java's List<? super T>. The lab's tests check exactly that.

sections.h: Declare variance once when you can, project when you must
sections.html:
You now have two places to put out and in, and the rule for choosing is short.

If every public member of a class only produces T, declare out T on the class. If every member only consumes T, declare in T. You do it once and every caller benefits: nobody writes a projection, and a List<Int> simply is a List<Number>. This is declaration-site variance, and it's why Kotlin code has far fewer wildcards than Java code.

If the class both reads and writes T, it stays invariant: MutableList, Array, a cache, a repository with save and findById. Then each function that only reads, or only writes, asks for a projection:

Java
static final class Ledger<T> {                   // reads and writes T: invariant
    private final List<T> entries = new ArrayList<>();
    void record(T entry) { entries.add(entry); }
    T latest() { return entries.get(entries.size() - 1); }
}

static String latestId(Ledger<? extends PaymentEvent> ledger) { return ledger.latest().getPaymentId(); }
static void recordCard(Ledger<? super CardAuthorized> ledger, String id, long cents) {
    ledger.record(new CardAuthorized(id, cents));
}
Kotlin
class Ledger<T> {                                // reads and writes T: invariant
    private val entries = mutableListOf<T>()
    fun record(entry: T) { entries += entry }
    fun latest(): T = entries.last()
}

fun latestId(ledger: Ledger<out PaymentEvent>): String = ledger.latest().paymentId
fun recordCard(ledger: Ledger<in CardAuthorized>, id: String, cents: Long) =
    ledger.record(CardAuthorized(id, cents))

Java has no declaration-site variance, so every Java API works like Ledger. Each method that only reads or only writes must remember its wildcard, and the JDK has hundreds of them. Forget one and your own tests still pass. The first caller with a List<Integer> finds out.

The Kotlin compiler also guards the line between the two kinds:

You write The compiler says
List<out PaymentEvent> warning: Projection is redundant: the corresponding type parameter of 'List<out PaymentEvent>' has the same variance.
List<in PaymentEvent> error: Projection conflicts with variance of the corresponding type parameter of 'List<in PaymentEvent>'. Remove the projection or replace it with '*'.
fun <out T> onFunction(t: T) error: Variance annotations are only allowed for type parameters of classes and interfaces.

The last one catches people. Variance says when a C<A> can stand in for a C<B>. A generic function is not a type you can substitute, so out on its own type parameter has nothing to describe. Put the projection on a parameter's type instead, as copyInto does. The '*' in the second message is the star projection, the subject of the next lesson.

Java has only use-site variance, so every class is like Ledger: * invariant, with ? extends or ? super written by each method that only reads or only writes. */ public class ChooseDemoJava { static final class Ledger<T> { private final List<T> entries = new ArrayList<>(); void record(T entry) { entries.add(entry); } T latest() { return entries.get(entries.size() - 1); } } // only reads: ? extends static String latestId(Ledger<? extends PaymentEvent> ledger) { return ledger.latest().getPaymentId(); } // only writes cards: ? super static void recordCard(Ledger<? super CardAuthorized> ledger, String id, long cents) { ledger.record(new CardAuthorized(id, cents)); } public static void main(String[] args) { Ledger<CardAuthorized> cards = new Ledger<>(); Ledger<PaymentEvent> everything = new Ledger<>(); everything.record(new RefundIssued("pay_1", 500)); recordCard(cards, "pay_2", 1_200); recordCard(everything, "pay_3", 350); System.out.println(latestId(cards) + " " + latestId(everything)); // Wrong move: the class is invariant, so the plain type still doesn't fit. // Ledger<PaymentEvent> strict = cards; } }

try.expect: Both print pay_2 pay_3. The wrong move fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Ledger<PaymentEvent>', actual 'Ledger<CardAuthorized>'. (Java: Ledger<CardAuthorized> cannot be converted to Ledger<PaymentEvent>): the projections are on the functions, not the class. Line 1 compiles with the Projection is redundant warning. Line 2 fails with Projection conflicts with variance of the corresponding type parameter of 'List<in PaymentEvent>'. Line 3 fails with Variance annotations are only allowed for type parameters of classes and interfaces.

analogy: Think of an invariant MutableList as a shared ledger book in the finance office. The book itself allows reading and writing. A use-site projection is a permission slip for one visit. An out-projection is a reading-room pass: you may read every entry, and you're told only that each one is "some kind of number", so you are not allowed to write anything in. An in-projection is the drop slot in the door: you can post an entry of the agreed kind, and if you peek through the slot you see only "something". The book never changes; only what this visitor may do changes. The analogy breaks in one place: a reading-room pass in real life also stops you from tearing pages out, but an out-projection does not. clear() and removeAt() still work, because a projection limits types, not mutation.
world: Use-site projections show up at the edges of a payment service, where you pass mutable buffers around. A Kafka batch listener collects records into a MutableList<PaymentEvent> and hands it to helpers: the fee calculator only reads, so it takes MutableList<out PaymentEvent> (or better, a plain List), and the enrichment step only appends CardAuthorized lines, so it takes MutableList<in CardAuthorized>. Your own invariant classes get the same treatment: a Quarkus-managed Ledger<T> or a Cache<K, V> with get and put stays invariant, and the report that only reads asks for Cache<String, out Money>. On the Java side of the codebase, the same contracts are List<? extends PaymentEvent> and List<? super CardAuthorized>, the shape of the JDK's Collections.addAll(Collection<? super T> c, T... elements).
mistake: The common mistake is declaring a parameter MutableList<Number> (Java: List<Number>) when the function only reads it. It works for the first caller, who happens to have a list of Number. The next caller has a MutableList<Int> and fixes the type error with ints.toMutableList<Number>(), an unchecked cast, or a second copy of the function. People make the mistake because the plain type looks simpler, and because "an Int is a Number" makes it feel like it should work. The fix is to ask what the function does with the list. Only reads and never modifies: take a read-only List<Number>. Reads and also removes or clears: take MutableList<out Number>. Only adds: take MutableList<in Int>. Reads and adds: keep the plain type.

compare.title: The same copy and fill contracts with wildcards and with projections

java.title: Transfers.java
java.html: import java.util.List; import java.util.Queue; import java.util.Collection; final class Transfers { // dest only takes T, src only gives T: the shape of Collections.copy static <T> int copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); return from.size(); } // only writes: ? super static <T> void fillWith(List<? super T> target, T value, int count) { for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(value); } // a read-only parameter still needs ? extends in Java static double sumAll(List<? extends Number> amounts) { double sum = 0; for (Number a : amounts) sum += a.doubleValue(); return sum; } }

kotlin.title: Projections.kt
kotlin.html: // MutableList is invariant, so each function projects it at the use site fun <T> copyInto(from: MutableList<out T>, to: MutableList<in T>): Int { for (x in from) to.add(x) return from.size } fun <T> fillWith(target: MutableList<in T>, value: T, count: Int) { repeat(count) { target.add(value) } } // List is declared List<out E>: no projection needed (one would only earn a warning) fun sumAll(amounts: List<Number>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (a in amounts) sum += a.toDouble() return sum }

compare.note: For MutableList, the two versions say exactly the same thing: Kotlin's MutableList<out T> compiles to Java's List<? extends T>, and MutableList<in T> to List<? super T>, and Kotlin shows Java's wildcards back to you as out and in. The real difference is sumAll. Java has no read-only list type with declared variance, so every reading parameter needs ? extends. Kotlin's List carries out E on its declaration, so the plain type is already flexible and a projection on it is redundant. Arrays differ too: Java arrays are covariant with run-time store checks and take no wildcards, while Kotlin's Array<out T> is a compile-time projection that compiles down to a plain Java array.

worked.title: Settle pending authorizations into a batch of any events

steps.say: A settlement job moves pending card authorizations into the outgoing batch, then clears the pending list. The first draft uses plain types. The batch the caller has is a MutableList<PaymentEvent>, because it also holds refunds. Read the error.
steps.code: fun settle(pending: MutableList<CardAuthorized>, batch: MutableList<CardAuthorized>): Long { var cents = 0L for (a in pending) { batch.add(a); cents += a.cents } pending.clear() return cents } val pending = mutableListOf(CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200), CardAuthorized("pay_2", 350)) val batch = mutableListOf<PaymentEvent>(RefundIssued("pay_0", 500)) settle(pending, batch) // error: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<PaymentEvent>', // but 'MutableList<CardAuthorized>' was expected.

alt.html: static long settle(List<CardAuthorized> pending, List<CardAuthorized> batch) { long cents = 0; for (CardAuthorized a : pending) { batch.add(a); cents += a.cents(); } pending.clear(); return cents; } List<CardAuthorized> pending = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200), new CardAuthorized("pay_2", 350))); List<PaymentEvent> batch = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new RefundIssued("pay_0", 500))); settle(pending, batch); // error: incompatible types: List<PaymentEvent> cannot be converted to List<CardAuthorized>

steps.say: Name what each parameter does with CardAuthorized values. pending gives them to you (and is cleared, which takes no element). batch only receives them. So pending is a producer and batch is a consumer, for this function only. Both types are MutableList, which can't be declared out or in, so the variance goes on the parameters.
Project each parameter. Self-check before reading the comments: why does pending.clear() still compile through an out-projection? (It takes no E, so it can't smuggle a wrong type in.)
steps.code: fun settle(pending: MutableList<out CardAuthorized>, batch: MutableList<in CardAuthorized>): Long { var cents = 0L for (a in pending) { // 1. read: each a is a CardAuthorized batch.add(a) // 2. write: the batch takes CardAuthorized or anything above it cents += a.cents } pending.clear() // 3. no E in clear(), so the read view allows it return cents } settle(pending, batch) // compiles: 1550, and batch holds the refund plus both cards

alt.html: static long settle(List<? extends CardAuthorized> pending, List<? super CardAuthorized> batch) { long cents = 0; for (CardAuthorized a : pending) { // 1. read: producer extends batch.add(a); // 2. write: consumer super cents += a.cents(); } pending.clear(); // 3. no T in clear() return cents; } settle(pending, batch); // compiles

steps.say: Check the result from the caller's side. The batch can now be a MutableList<CardAuthorized>, a MutableList<PaymentEvent> or a MutableList<Any>. The pending list can be a list of any subtype of CardAuthorized. If you later need settle to read back from the batch (say, to dedupe by payment id), that read returns Any? through the in-projection, and the compiler tells you so. At that point the parameter really is read and write, and it should go back to the plain type.

lab.title: Project MutableList at the use site, then do it in Java
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail. The signature tests print what Java sees today, such as but was: "List<T>": no projection means no wildcard.
In Projections.kt, give copyInto's from an out and its to an in, then write the loop and return the count.
Give fillWith's target the projection that matches "only written", then append count copies.
Write sumAll. Then change its parameter to List<out Number>, run the tests, and find the warning in the output. Put the plain List<Number> back.
In Transfers.java, change drainTo's parameters to Queue<? extends T> and Collection<? super T>, then poll until the queue is empty.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: for (x in from) to.add(x) type-checks because a read from MutableList<out T> gives a T, and MutableList<in T> accepts a T.
Queue.poll() returns null when the queue is empty: for (T item = from.poll(); item != null; item = from.poll()).
Why does sumAll(ints) compile before you touch it? Because Kotlin's List is declared List<out E>. Only MutableList needs the projection.

drill.title: Write copyInto and its Java signature from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write copyInto(from, to) for two MutableLists in Kotlin, with the projections that let a MutableList<Int> be copied into a MutableList<Number>. Then write the Java method that Kotlin generates for it (the signature is enough), and the Java version of fillWith.

answer.html: fun <T> copyInto(from: MutableList<out T>, to: MutableList<in T>): Int { for (x in from) to.add(x) // reads give T, writes take T return from.size } fun <T> fillWith(target: MutableList<in T>, value: T, count: Int) { repeat(count) { target.add(value) } } // Java sees: public static <T> int copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) // public static <T> void fillWith(List<? super T> target, T value, int count)

alt.title: Transfers.java
alt.html: static <T> int copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); // producer extends, consumer super return from.size(); } static <T> void fillWith(List<? super T> target, T value, int count) { for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(value); }

recap: A type that both reads and writes T (MutableList, Array, your own Ledger) must stay invariant.
A type projection adds out or in at one use: MutableList<out Number> is a read view, MutableList<in Int> is a write view.
Through an out-projection reads give the bound and calls that take T are forbidden. Through an in-projection writes of T are allowed and reads give only Any?.
Kotlin's out T / in T projections compile to Java's ? extends T / ? super T, and Java's wildcards show up in Kotlin as out and in.
Declare variance on the class when every member only produces or only consumes T. Project at the use site when the class does both.
Projecting an already-variant type earns a warning (List<out T>) or an error (List<in T>), and variance on a function's type parameter is an error.

explain.prompt: A teammate's fun total(amounts: MutableList<Number>) rejects their MutableList<Int>. They propose making MutableList covariant "like List". Explain why that can't work, and what to write instead.
explain.answer: MutableList has add(element: E) as well as get(): E, so E is in an in-position and an out-position. If a MutableList<Int> could be used as a MutableList<Number>, someone could add a Double to a list of ints, which is exactly the bug Java arrays have. So the class has to stay invariant. But total only reads, so it can ask for a read-only view in its own signature: MutableList<out Number>. That accepts a list of any subtype of Number, gives back Number on reads, and forbids add. Even simpler, if total never modifies the list, take a plain read-only List<Number>, which is already covariant. In Java the same parameter is List<? extends Number>.

deeper.html:
Both compilers turn a wildcard or projection into a fresh captured type each time they check an expression: "the one specific type this list really has". That's why CAP#1 shows up in javac messages. Java can also capture a wildcard for a method call, which gives a well-known trick: you can't write l.set(i, l.get(j)) on a List<?>, but you can pass the List<?> to a private generic helper <T> void swapHelper(List<T> l, int i, int j), and inside the helper the element type has a name. The JDK chose not to bother. Collections.swap(List<?> list, int i, int j) assigns the list to a raw List and calls l.set(i, l.set(j, l.get(i))) under @SuppressWarnings, with a source comment saying that capturing the wildcard would need a supplementary private method.

Kotlin captures projected arguments for calls too. Given fun <T> swap(l: MutableList<T>, i: Int, j: Int), the calls swap(star, 0, 1) with star: MutableList<*> and swap(view, 0, 1) with view: MutableList<out Number> both compile with kotlinc 2.4.21. Inside swap, T is the captured type, so values read from the list may be written back into the same list. You'll meet MutableList<*> properly in the next lesson.

Arrays have one more twist. Because Java arrays carry no wildcards, Kotlin compiles Array<out Number> and Array<Number> both to Number[], and Array<in Number> to Object[]. From Java, those differences are invisible; the projection exists only for the Kotlin compiler. The door opens the other way too. Kotlin shows a Java Object[] parameter as Array<(out) Any!>!, so you may pass an Array<String> to it, as Java code could. That brings Java's covariance back: java.util.Arrays.fill(names, 42) with names: Array<String> compiles in Kotlin and throws ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer at run time.
